groups.title: Relational data modeling and normalization
groups.question: You are designing tables for a recipe app with users, recipes, ingredients and categories. Explain how you would organize the data and keep it consistent.

followUps.Normalization: splitting data to elimina: What problem does normalization solve, and can it go too far?
followUps.Primary keys, foreign keys, and referent: What does a foreign key guarantee, and what happens when you delete a parent row?

evidence.text: Normalization splits data into tables so each fact is stored once.
This avoids update problems where the same data must be changed in many places.
Too much normalization needs many joins for reads, so some duplication can be a deliberate trade-off.
A foreign key guarantees the referenced row exists.
ON DELETE CASCADE removes child rows when the parent is deleted.
ON DELETE RESTRICT blocks deleting a parent that still has children.

notEnough: Only saying foreign keys link tables.

groups.title: SQL query execution model
groups.question: You need a report of every category with its number of recipes, including categories with none, but only categories with more than five. Explain how you would write it in SQL.

followUps.How JOIN operations combine rows from mu: Why would an INNER JOIN drop categories with no recipes, and what would you use instead?
followUps.GROUP BY with aggregate functions and th: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

evidence.text: An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables.
A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills missing matches with NULL.
For categories with no recipes, a LEFT JOIN from categories is needed.
GROUP BY collapses rows with the same value into groups so aggregates like COUNT can be computed.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.
HAVING filters the groups after aggregation, such as keeping counts above five.

notEnough: Only saying HAVING is like WHERE for groups.

groups.title: Writing SQL and connecting to PostgreSQL from Node
groups.question: Your Node API builds SQL strings from user input and opens a new database connection for every request. Explain the risks and how you would fix both.

followUps.SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE with para: Why must you use parameterized queries instead of building SQL strings?
followUps.Connection pooling with the pg Pool clas: Why use a connection pool instead of a new connection per request?

evidence.text: Putting user input into SQL strings lets attackers change the query, which is SQL injection.
Parameterized queries send values separately from the SQL, so input is never run as code.
They also let the database reuse query plans.

notEnough: Only saying parameterized queries are safer.

evidence.text: Opening a database connection is slow and uses resources on the database.
A pool keeps connections open and reuses them across requests.
The pool caps the number of connections and queues extra queries.

groups.title: Indexes and constraints for data integrity
groups.question: Filtering recipes by category gets slow as the table grows, and duplicate user emails and negative prices keep appearing in the data. Explain how indexes and constraints help.

followUps.Creating indexes on columns used in WHER: How would you speed up the category filter and check that it worked?
followUps.UNIQUE and CHECK constraints for data in: Why enforce unique emails and positive prices in the database, not only in the app?

evidence.text: Without an index, the database scans every row.
An index on the filtered or joined column lets the database find rows quickly.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows whether the index is actually used.

notEnough: Only saying indexes make queries faster.

misconceptions.text: Says adding an index to every column has no downside.

evidence.text: A UNIQUE constraint stops duplicate values like emails.
A CHECK constraint enforces rules like price greater than zero.
Database constraints catch bad data even when application validation is missed or bypassed.

notEnough: Only saying constraints keep data valid.
